learningObjectives.title: Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields
Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid

questions.q: Which of the following is a magnetic material?
questions.explain: The magnetic materials are iron, steel, cobalt and nickel; copper, aluminium and brass are non-magnetic.

questions.q: In which direction do magnetic field lines point outside a bar magnet?
options: From the north pole to the south pole
From the south pole to the north pole
From both poles towards the centre
Away from the magnet in all directions equally
questions.explain: By convention, field lines run from north to south outside the magnet, showing the direction a north pole would be pushed.

questions.q: When an unmagnetised piece of iron becomes an induced magnet in a magnetic field, the force between it and the magnet is always:
questions.explain: Induced magnetism always produces a force of attraction, and the induced magnetism is lost once the material is removed from the field.

questions.q: Where is a bar magnet's magnetic field strongest?
options: At the centre of the magnet
The field has the same strength everywhere
questions.explain: The field is strongest at the poles, shown by the field lines being closest together there.

questions.q: Two magnets are brought together so that a north pole faces a north pole. What happens?
options: There is no force between them
questions.explain: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract; this is a non-contact force.

questions.q: What does the behaviour of a magnetic compass provide evidence for?
options: That the Earth has a magnetic field, produced by its core
That the compass needle is radioactive
questions.explain: A compass needle aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, which is generated by the Earth's core.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of an electromagnet compared with a permanent magnet?
options: Its magnetism can be switched on and off using the current
It produces a field without any coil
questions.explain: An electromagnet (a solenoid, usually with an iron core) is magnetic only while current flows, so it can be controlled.

questions.q: What is the unit of magnetic flux density?
questions.explain: Magnetic flux density B is measured in tesla (T).

questions.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the first finger (forefinger) represent?
questions.explain: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force).

questions.q: A current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field. When is the force on the wire zero?
options: When the wire is parallel to the magnetic field
When the wire is at right angles to the field
questions.explain: The motor-effect force is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel to it.

questions.q: A 0.50 m wire carries a current of 4.0 A and experiences a force of 0.60 N when perpendicular to a magnetic field. What is the magnetic flux density?
questions.explain: Rearranging F = BIL gives B = F / (IL) = 0.60 / (4.0 x 0.50) = 0.30 T.

questions.q: A wire of length 0.20 m carries a current of 5.0 A at right angles to a field of flux density 0.30 T. What is the force on the wire?
What is the purpose of the split-ring commutator in a simple d.c. motor?
options: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction
It increases the voltage supplied to the coil
It converts alternating current into a magnetic field
It stops the coil from overheating
questions.explain: Reversing the current each half-turn keeps the force acting to spin the coil continuously in one direction.

questions.q: What happens when a magnet is moved into a coil of wire connected in a complete circuit?
options: A potential difference is induced and a current flows
The coil becomes a permanent magnet
Nothing happens unless the coil is heated
questions.explain: The generator effect induces a potential difference across a conductor when there is relative movement in a magnetic field; a complete circuit allows a current.

questions.q: Which change would increase the size of the potential difference induced in a generator?
options: Using fewer turns on the coil
questions.explain: The induced p.d. increases with faster relative movement, a stronger field and more turns on the coil.

questions.q: A transformer is 100% efficient. Its secondary output is 12 V at 2.0 A and its primary is connected to 240 V. What is the primary current?
questions.explain: For 100% efficiency, Vp x Ip = Vs x Is, so Ip = (12 x 2.0) / 240 = 0.10 A.

questions.q: In the generator effect, what happens to the induced potential difference if the direction of movement of the magnet is reversed?
options: The induced potential difference reverses direction
The induced potential difference falls to zero
questions.explain: Reversing the movement (or the poles) reverses the direction of the induced p.d. and current.

questions.q: Which equation correctly relates the voltages and turns of a transformer?
options: Vp x Vs = Np x Ns
questions.explain: The ratio of primary to secondary p.d. equals the ratio of primary to secondary turns.

questions.q: Why does the National Grid transmit electrical power at very high voltage?
options: A higher voltage means a lower current, which reduces energy wasted as heat in the cables
A higher voltage makes the electrons travel faster
A higher voltage prevents the wires from breaking
A higher voltage increases the current in the cables
questions.explain: Step-up transformers raise the voltage so the current is smaller, greatly reducing heating losses in the transmission cables.

questions.q: A transformer has 800 turns on the primary and 200 turns on the secondary. If the primary p.d. is 240 V, what is the secondary p.d.?
questions.explain: Using Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, Vs = Vp x Ns/Np = 240 x 200/800 = 60 V (a step-down transformer).
